items.stem: The law of diminishing returns states that
options: as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the marginal product of the variable factor will eventually fall
as a firm grows, its long-run average cost rises
returns fall when all factors are increased in proportion
total product falls as soon as more workers are employed
items.answer: as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the marginal product of the variable factor will eventually fall
items.markingKey: Short-run law: at least one factor fixed; MP eventually declines.

items.stem: Explain why the law of diminishing returns applies only in the short run.
items.answer: It depends on at least one factor (e.g. capital or land) being fixed; with more workers sharing the fixed factor, each extra worker eventually adds less. In the long run all factors can be varied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed factor needed; 1 mark: crowding of fixed factor; 1 mark: LR all variable [3]

items.stem: Explain the relationship between marginal product and the marginal cost curve.
items.answer: With a constant wage, MC = wage/MP. When MP rises, MC falls; once diminishing returns set in and MP falls, MC rises, giving a U-shaped MC curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC = W/MP; 1 mark: rising MP lowers MC, falling MP raises MC [2]

items.stem: Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total product (bicycles per day): 15, 38, 57, 73, 85, 92, 93. Calculate the average product when 2 workers are employed.
items.answer: 19 bicycles

items.stem: A small factory with a fixed amount of machinery employs workers as follows. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total product (meals per day): 10, 26, 46, 62, 72, 77, 76. (a) Calculate the marginal and average product for each number of workers. (b) Identify the worker at which diminishing marginal returns set in and explain why they occur.
items.answer: (a) MP: 10, 16, 20, 16, 10, 5, -1; AP: 10, 13, 15.3, 15.5, 14.4, 12.8, 10.9 (b) From worker 4: MP falls because extra workers share a fixed stock of machinery.
items.markingKey: (a) MP = ΔTP [2], AP = TP/L [1]; (b) diminishing returns where MP first falls [1]; fixed factor explanation [1].

items.stem: Silverline makes bottled water in Halvoria and sells in a competitive market at $33 per unit. Fixed costs are $80 thousand. Output (000 units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($000): 112, 135, 155, 178, 210, 257. (a) Calculate the marginal cost of each thousand units. (b) Explain why marginal cost eventually rises in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 32, 23, 20, 23, 32, 47 (b) Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor: each extra worker adds less output, so the cost of each extra unit rises.

items.stem: Explain why average product rises when marginal product is greater than average product.
items.answer: If the extra worker adds more than the current average, the average must rise (like a high mark raising a class average).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: marginal above average; 1 mark: pulls the average up [2]

items.stem: Which cost does not change as output changes in the short run?
items.answer: Total fixed cost
items.markingKey: TFC (e.g. rent, interest) is independent of output in the SR.

items.stem: Explain why the short-run average total cost curve is U-shaped.
items.answer: At low output AFC falls rapidly and increasing returns lower AVC, so ATC falls; beyond a point diminishing returns raise AVC and MC by more than AFC falls, so ATC rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: falling AFC; 1 mark: increasing then diminishing returns to variable factor; 1 mark: net effect [3]

items.stem: Explain why the gap between ATC and AVC narrows as output rises.
items.answer: The gap is AFC = TFC/Q, which falls as fixed costs are spread over more units.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gap = AFC; 1 mark: spreading fixed cost [2]

items.stem: A firm has total fixed cost of $80. Its total variable cost at outputs 1 to 6 is: 18, 32, 50, 80, 130, 208 ($). Calculate the average total cost at an output of 2 units.

A firm’s short-run costs are shown. At zero output total cost is $80. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($): 106, 120, 130, 144, 170, 216. (a) Calculate TFC, AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at each output. (b) Identify the output at which MC cuts ATC and explain why.
items.answer: (a) TFC = $80; AFC: 80, 40, 26.7, 20, 16, 13.3; AVC: 26, 20, 16.7, 16, 18, 22.7; ATC: 106, 60, 43.3, 36, 34, 36; MC: 26, 14, 10, 14, 26, 46. (b) Near the minimum of ATC (output 5), because when MC < ATC the average falls and when MC > ATC it rises.
items.markingKey: (a) TFC = TC at Q = 0 [1]; AFC, AVC, ATC divisions [2]; MC differences [1]; (b) MC cuts ATC at its minimum, with reason [2].

items.stem: A firm’s short-run costs are shown. At zero output total cost is $60. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($): 76, 90, 106, 128, 160, 206. (a) Calculate TFC, AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at each output. (b) Identify the output at which MC cuts ATC and explain why.
items.answer: (a) TFC = $60; AFC: 60, 30, 20, 15, 12, 10; AVC: 16, 15, 15.3, 17, 20, 24.3; ATC: 76, 45, 35.3, 32, 32, 34.3; MC: 16, 14, 16, 22, 32, 46. (b) Near the minimum of ATC (output 4), because when MC < ATC the average falls and when MC > ATC it rises.
items.markingKey: (a) TFC = TC at Q = 0 [1]; AFC, AVC, ATC divisions [2]; MC differences [1]; (b) MC cuts ATC at its minimum, with reason [2].

(b) Explain why marginal cost eventually rises in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 64, 41, 32.7, 29, 28, 29; minimum at 5 (b) Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor: each extra worker adds less output, so the cost of each extra unit rises.
items.markingKey: (a) ATC = TC/Q [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Juniper Brands makes fresh fruit in Loristan and sells in a competitive market at $37 per unit. Fixed costs are $100 thousand. Output (000 units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($000): 124, 144, 168, 204, 260, 344. (a) Calculate average total cost at each output and identify its minimum. (b) Identify the profit-maximising output and calculate the profit.
items.answer: (a) 124, 72, 56, 51, 52, 57.3; minimum at 4 (b) 4 thousand units; loss minimised at $56 thousand
items.markingKey: (a) ATC = TC/Q [2] (b) Max of TR − TC (or P = MC): TR = 37×4, profit = -56 [3]

items.stem: Average fixed cost always
items.answer: falls as output rises
items.markingKey: AFC = TFC/Q, so it falls continuously (spreading overheads).

items.stem: A firm has total fixed cost of $50. Its total variable cost at outputs 1 to 6 is: 20, 36, 56, 88, 140, 220 ($). Calculate the average variable cost at an output of 6 units.
Economies of scale occur when
options: total cost falls as output rises
short-run average cost falls as more workers are hired
long-run average cost falls as the scale of output increases
items.answer: long-run average cost falls as the scale of output increases
items.markingKey: Internal EoS: lower LRAC from growth of the firm.

items.stem: Explain two types of internal economies of scale.
items.answer: Technical: larger, more efficient machinery and the law of increased dimensions; Purchasing: bulk-buying discounts; Financial: cheaper borrowing; Managerial: specialist managers; Risk-bearing: diversification. Each lowers LRAC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each type, 1 mark each explanation of lower unit cost [4]

items.stem: Explain why the long-run average cost curve is often L-shaped rather than U-shaped in practice.
items.answer: Economies of scale are exhausted at the MES, but firms may avoid diseconomies through decentralisation and technology, so LRAC stays roughly constant over a wide range of output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: falling LRAC to MES; 1 mark: diseconomies avoided, constant beyond [2]

items.stem: A firm’s long-run average cost schedule is: Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; LRAC ($): 65, 60, 55, 50, 45, 45, 49. What is the minimum efficient scale of production?
items.answer: 50 thousand units
items.markingKey: MES = lowest output at which LRAC reaches its minimum ($45): 50 thousand units.

items.stem: A firm’s long-run average cost schedule is: Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; LRAC ($): 60, 55, 50, 50, 54, 58, 59. (a) Identify the minimum efficient scale and the range of output with diseconomies of scale. (b) Calculate the percentage cost disadvantage of a firm producing 20 thousand units compared with a firm at the MES.
items.answer: (a) MES = 30 thousand units; diseconomies from above 40 thousand units (LRAC rises). (b) (55 − 50)/55 × 100 = 9.1% higher unit cost.
items.markingKey: (a) MES identified [1]; rising LRAC = diseconomies [1]; (b) correct % calculation [2].

items.stem: A firm’s long-run average cost schedule is: Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; LRAC ($): 75, 70, 65, 60, 60, 64, 66. (a) Identify the minimum efficient scale and the range of output with diseconomies of scale. (b) Calculate the percentage cost disadvantage of a firm producing 30 thousand units compared with a firm at the MES. (c) Total market demand is 60 thousand units. Calculate how many firms of minimum efficient scale the market can support and comment on the likely market structure.
items.answer: (a) MES = 40 thousand units; diseconomies from above 50 thousand units (LRAC rises). (b) (65 − 60)/65 × 100 = 7.7% higher unit cost. (c) 60/40 = 1.5 firms; few firms → oligopoly or natural monopoly.
items.markingKey: (a) MES identified [1]; rising LRAC = diseconomies [1]; (b) correct % calculation [2]. (c) market size ÷ MES [1]; structure inference [1].

items.answer: (a) 62, 37.5, 28.3, 24.5, 24, 26.2; minimum at 5 (b) Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor: each extra worker adds less output, so the cost of each extra unit rises.

items.stem: Distinguish between diminishing returns and diseconomies of scale.
items.answer: Diminishing returns is a short-run concept with at least one factor fixed (MP falls); diseconomies of scale occur in the long run when all factors vary and LRAC rises as the firm grows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Normal profit is
options: the minimum profit needed to keep a firm in the industry, included in average cost
the maximum profit a firm can make
items.answer: the minimum profit needed to keep a firm in the industry, included in average cost
items.markingKey: Normal profit = opportunity cost of the entrepreneur; AR = ATC.

items.stem: Explain the relationship between price elasticity of demand and marginal revenue.
items.answer: Where demand is price elastic, a price cut raises TR so MR > 0; at unit elasticity MR = 0 and TR is at a maximum; where demand is inelastic, MR < 0.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each region [3]

items.stem: Explain why normal profit is treated as a cost.
items.answer: It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur’s time and capital: the return needed to keep resources in this use rather than the next best alternative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: opportunity cost; 1 mark: needed to keep firm in industry [2]

items.stem: A firm faces the demand schedule: price ($) 78, 76, 74, 72, 70, 68, 66 for quantities 1 to 7. Calculate the marginal revenue of unit 4.

A firm faces this demand schedule: quantity 1 to 7; price ($) 48, 46, 44, 42, 40, 38, 36. (a) Calculate total and marginal revenue at each output. (b) At an output of 4 units, average total cost (including normal profit) is $37. Calculate the profit and state the type of profit earned.
items.markingKey: (a) TR = P × Q [1], MR = ΔTR [1]; (b) profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1]; correct classification [1].

items.stem: A firm faces this demand schedule: quantity 1 to 7; price ($) 67, 62, 57, 52, 47, 42, 37. (a) Calculate total and marginal revenue at each output. (b) At an output of 5 units, average total cost (including normal profit) is $44. Calculate the profit and state the type of profit earned. (c) Identify the output that maximises total revenue and explain what this tells you about price elasticity of demand at that point.
items.answer: (a) TR: 67, 124, 171, 208, 235, 252, 259; MR: 67, 57, 47, 37, 27, 17, 7 (b) (47 − 44) × 5 = $15: supernormal profit. (c) TR is highest at 7 units, where MR ≈ 0, so PED ≈ 1 (unit elastic) there; demand is elastic above that price and inelastic below it.
items.markingKey: (a) TR = P × Q [1], MR = ΔTR [1]; (b) profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1]; correct classification [1]. (c) TR max where MR = 0 [1]; unit elasticity [1].

items.stem: Explain why supernormal profit may be competed away in the long run in some markets but not in others.
items.answer: Where barriers to entry are low, supernormal profit attracts new firms, shifting each firm’s demand left until AR = ATC; where barriers are high (monopoly, oligopoly), entry is blocked and profit persists.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: entry signal; 1 mark: demand shifts until normal profit; 1 mark: barriers prevent this [3]

items.stem: Marginal product of labour is
options: the change in total product from employing one more worker
total product divided by the number of workers
the wage paid to the last worker
the revenue from the last worker
items.answer: the change in total product from employing one more worker
items.markingKey: MP = ΔTP/ΔL.

items.stem: The marginal cost curve cuts the average total cost curve
options: at the minimum point of average total cost
items.answer: at the minimum point of average total cost

items.stem: Explain why a firm might continue to produce in the short run even though it is making a loss.
items.answer: If price covers average variable cost, each unit makes a contribution to fixed costs, which must be paid anyway; shutting down would make the loss larger (equal to TFC).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: P ≥ AVC; 1 mark: contribution to fixed costs [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the gap between ATC and AVC narrows as output rises. (b) Explain why the short-run average total cost curve is U-shaped.

items.stem: Which is an example of an external economy of scale?

Bulk-buying discounts for a large supermarket

items.stem: Many electricity supply firms in Jovania have clustered around Auckland. Explain how they may benefit from external economies of scale.
items.answer: Industry growth in one area gives a pool of skilled labour, specialist suppliers and services, shared infrastructure and knowledge spillovers, lowering costs for every firm.

items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Large firms reach MES and enjoy economies of scale. items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the gap between ATC and AVC narrows as output rises. (b) Explain why the short-run average total cost curve is U-shaped.
items.answer: (a) The gap is AFC = TFC/Q, which falls as fixed costs are spread over more units. (b) At low output AFC falls rapidly and increasing returns lower AVC, so ATC falls; beyond a point diminishing returns raise AVC and MC by more than AFC falls, so ATC rises.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: gap = AFC; 1 mark: spreading fixed cost [2] (b) 1 mark: falling AFC; 1 mark: increasing then diminishing returns to variable factor; 1 mark: net effect [3]

items.stem: A firm has total fixed cost of $80. Its total variable cost at outputs 1 to 6 is: 28, 44, 56, 72, 100, 148 ($). Calculate the average total cost at an output of 5 units.

A firm’s short-run costs are shown. At zero output total cost is $120. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($): 141, 159, 180, 210, 255, 321. (a) Calculate TFC, AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at each output. (b) Identify the output at which MC cuts ATC and explain why.
items.answer: (a) TFC = $120; AFC: 120, 60, 40, 30, 24, 20; AVC: 21, 19.5, 20, 22.5, 27, 33.5; ATC: 141, 79.5, 60, 52.5, 51, 53.5; MC: 21, 18, 21, 30, 45, 66. (b) Near the minimum of ATC (output 5), because when MC < ATC the average falls and when MC > ATC it rises.
items.markingKey: (a) TFC = TC at Q = 0 [1]; AFC, AVC, ATC divisions [2]; MC differences [1]; (b) MC cuts ATC at its minimum, with reason [2].

items.stem: Silverline reports a loss for the second year running as demand for restaurant meals falls. Consider whether a firm should close down if it is making a loss.
items.answer: Arguments for: In the short run the firm should continue if P ≥ AVC because it covers some fixed costs; close if P < AVC. Arguments against / evaluation: In the long run must cover ATC; expectations of future demand; strategic reasons (market share, loss leaders); exit costs. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: The minimum efficient scale is
options: the smallest output a firm can produce
the output where marginal cost is zero
the output where the firm makes maximum profit
the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
items.answer: the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
items.markingKey: MES: where LRAC first reaches its minimum.

items.stem: Many brewing firms in Marvona have clustered around Nairobi. Explain how they may benefit from external economies of scale.
items.answer: Industry growth in one area gives a pool of skilled labour, specialist suppliers and services, shared infrastructure and knowledge spillovers, lowering costs for every firm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition (industry growth); 1 mark each example (up to 2) [3]

items.stem: A firm’s long-run average cost schedule is: Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; LRAC ($): 50, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 33. What is the minimum efficient scale of production?
items.answer: 50 thousand units
items.markingKey: MES = lowest output at which LRAC reaches its minimum ($30): 50 thousand units.

items.answer: 40 thousand units

items.stem: Fenwick & Co makes streaming subscriptions in Halvoria and sells in a competitive market at $29 per unit. Fixed costs are $100 thousand. Output (000 units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($000): 112, 122, 134, 152, 180, 222. (a) Calculate the marginal cost of each thousand units. (b) Explain why marginal cost eventually rises in the short run.
items.answer: (a) 12, 10, 12, 18, 28, 42 (b) Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor: each extra worker adds less output, so the cost of each extra unit rises.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the relationship between price elasticity of demand and marginal revenue. (b) Explain why normal profit is treated as a cost.
items.answer: (a) Where demand is price elastic, a price cut raises TR so MR > 0; at unit elasticity MR = 0 and TR is at a maximum; where demand is inelastic, MR < 0. (b) It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur’s time and capital: the return needed to keep resources in this use rather than the next best alternative.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each region [3] (b) 1 mark: opportunity cost; 1 mark: needed to keep firm in industry [2]

A firm faces this demand schedule: quantity 1 to 7; price ($) 76, 72, 68, 64, 60, 56, 52. (a) Calculate total and marginal revenue at each output. (b) At an output of 4 units, average total cost (including normal profit) is $57. Calculate the profit and state the type of profit earned.
items.markingKey: (a) TR = P × Q [1], MR = ΔTR [1]; (b) profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1]; correct classification [1].
